analysis.one_liner: Bans housing discrimination against renters who pay with vouchers, benefits, or other non-wage income.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House committee vote or floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added three new protected categories to the federal Fair Housing Act: source of income, veteran status, and military status. That means a landlord could not refuse to rent to someone simply because they pay with a housing voucher, Social Security or disability benefits, child support, or savings instead of a paycheck. It would also extend federal civil-rights protections against intimidation to these groups and extend the deadline for state and local housing agencies to keep enforcing fair-housing rules while they update their laws. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters whose lawful income comes from something other than a regular job: families and seniors using Section 8 housing vouchers, people receiving Social Security or disability benefits, veterans and active-duty service members, and people paying from child support, trusts, or savings. Landlords could no longer turn them away just because of how they pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voucher holders, veterans, and benefit recipients

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'source of income' to the Fair Housing Act's ban on housing discrimination, covering Section 8 vouchers, government and nonprofit rental assistance, Social Security and SSI benefits, Railroad Retirement benefits, court-ordered support payments, trust payments, and any other lawful income or savings [S2] [S3].
Adds veteran status and military status as protected categories, so landlords and lenders could not refuse housing or services to service members and veterans because of their status [S2] [S3].

Extends the criminal prohibition on intimidating or interfering with someone's housing rights to cover these three new categories, so threatening a voucher holder to make them leave would fall under the same federal law as racial intimidation in housing [S3].

Gives state and local fair-housing agencies a 40-month grace period (extendable by 6 months) to keep their existing certification while they update their laws to match the new protections, so enforcement does not lapse in the transition [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property owners lose some discretion over whom they rent to: they could no longer screen out tenants based on income source, veteran status, or military status. Rental-property owners would bear the cost of compliance and, in some cases, tenants whose payment relies on government subsidy programs. Some landlords argue voucher payment rules and inspection requirements add paperwork.

drawbacks.text: The bill restricts how landlords may screen tenants: a property owner who believes a voucher tenant's payment or inspection requirements create administrative burden could no longer decline those tenants categorically, which is exactly the screening practice the bill targets [S3].

The bill protects veteran- and military-specific programs from being challenged under the new rules (it explicitly shields lenders' veteran loan programs and federal veteran housing assistance), but it does not shield other targeted programs, and some fair-housing advocates argue carving out exceptions complicates enforcement [S3].

Extending the certification grace period for state and local fair-housing agencies delays the deadline for those jurisdictions to bring their own laws up to the new standard, which critics could view as slowing local compliance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit falls on lower-income renters and veterans, groups that are frequently refused housing when their income comes from vouchers or benefits rather than wages; that discrimination is well documented as a barrier to using housing assistance. The cost falls on landlords, who lose one screening tool and take on tenants whose payments may involve subsidy-program paperwork. The strongest objection is the compliance burden on small landlords, but the bill's carve-out for veteran-specific lending and housing programs limits collateral impact on other legitimate programs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which passed it along to a subcommittee, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters introduced the bill on June 26, 2019, joined by four original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S5].

On July 30, 2019, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, a standard step that often signals a bill is not moving toward a floor vote [S5].

No further action was taken: the bill never received a subcommittee or full committee vote, never reached the House floor, and was never taken up in the Senate before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rental-property owners are better off because the bill died: they kept the ability to refuse tenants based on income source or veteran status. Renters using vouchers or benefits gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split can only be inferred from sponsorship: all 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have barred landlords from rejecting tenants because their income comes from vouchers, benefits, or other non-wage sources. Landlords' interest in keeping that screening discretion runs directly against the renters the bill protects.

Lenders would be covered by the new anti-discrimination rules for real-estate-related transactions, but the bill explicitly protects veteran-specific loan programs, limiting the change for lenders serving veterans.
